facts.label: Financial base view
facts.text: The filed statements support a reliable financial base for Magnera Corporation, one consolidated entity, in USD millions across four balance-sheet dates (September 27, 2025, December 27, 2025, March 28, 2026 and June 27, 2026) and the flow periods FY2025, each FY2026 quarter, the nine months to June 27, 2026 and the matching nine months of FY2025. Every total and reconciliation tested foots to the filed statement, and the by-function expense block reconciles to operating income in each tested period (see Calculations). The base is limited, not blocked: earnings are measured on the company's adjusted EBITDA, which carries add-backs of about one third of the adjusted figure on an LTM basis; prior-year comparatives are carve-out and part-period (the Glatfelter business is consolidated only from November 4, 2024); interim cash interest and cash taxes are not reported, so cover uses a labelled proxy that ties exactly to the one reported annual cash interest figure; and the revolver is known only by size, maturity and a no-borrowings statement. Leverage and cover use gross debt principal as printed before the discount line and LTM adjusted EBITDA built from filed figures. No guidance, pro forma or synergy-adjusted release figure enters any ratio.

facts.label: Interpretation: evidence, risk mechanism, credit implication
facts.text: Leverage. Evidence: gross debt principal fell from 2,031 at September 27, 2025 to 1,966 at June 27, 2026 through repayments of the term loan (731 to 706) and the 7.25% notes (800 to 760) [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:8] "7.25% First Priority Senior Secured Notes November 2031 760 800", while LTM adjusted EBITDA rose from 354 to 372. Risk mechanism: both legs help, but the EBITDA is a company-defined measure and the gap to operating income plus D&A is 122 LTM. Credit implication: filed-basis leverage of 5.28x gross and 4.53x net is improving but remains above five times gross for a business that reports a net loss in every period shown. Higher LTM EBITDA contributed somewhat more of the improvement than debt repayment (calc: EBITDA change alone gives 5.46, debt change alone 5.55; see Calculations).

facts.label: Interpretation: evidence, risk mechanism, credit implication
facts.text: Add-backs and definition risk. Evidence: segment notes reconcile adjusted EBITDA to operating income through restructuring and integration charges, Argentina hyperinflation, carve-out allocation and other non-cash charges; the LTM restructuring and other activities charge was 81, and the nine-month charge of 61 splits into severance 13, facility exit 3, non-cash 10 and integration and other 35 [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:7] "Charges 13 3 10 35 61". The 10-K sized only the Project CORE capacity rationalisation at about 20 over two years [10-K_2025-09-27 page:15] "these actions are projected to cost approximately $20 million"; the charge line is therefore broader than that programme, and the integration and other component recurs each quarter, with a further 23 in Q3 including a loss on sale of a facility. Risk mechanism: add-backs that recur every quarter blur the line between non-recurring and operating cost; lenders and rating methodologies may haircut them. Credit implication: committee leverage should be shown on both bases (5.28x and 7.86x gross), and a covenant-style EBITDA cannot be inferred because no definition from an executed agreement is supplied.

facts.text: Interest cover. Evidence: net interest expense was 151 LTM against operating income of 63, so operating income covers interest 0.42 times; adjusted EBITDA covers the cash-interest proxy 2.91 times and net interest 2.46 times. Risk mechanism: floating-rate term loan exposure (the filing says a change of 0.25 percent changes annual interest expense by about 2) [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "A change of 0.25% on these floating interest rate exposures would increase our annual interest expense by approximately $2 million." Credit implication: cover is adequate only on the adjusted measure; lower SOFR (about 3.62 percent at June 27, 2026 against about 4.19 percent at September 27, 2025 per the filings) has helped the floating portion.

facts.label: Business and transaction view
facts.text: The supplied sources show a mid-sized, publicly listed manufacturer of nonwoven and film-based specialty materials for consumer-oriented end markets, formed in a combination in which a carve-out of the former parent's health, hygiene and specialties business merged with Glatfelter. The structure matters to a creditor in three ways. First, the combination was financed with new first priority secured debt and a cash distribution to the former parent, so opening leverage was set by the transaction rather than by operations; since closing the documented capital allocation is voluntary debt repayment, with no dividends or buybacks in the equity statements. Second, the integration is incomplete: the issuer reports material weaknesses tied to the merger and still depends on the former parent's legacy IT systems under a transition services agreement, so the reporting base is exposed to a counterparty that is also the former owner. Third, the operating model combines high input-cost pass-through with lag, a large customer concentration (top ten about 42 percent of FY2025 net sales) and a geographic mix in which Rest of World, the lower-margin segment, is the largest region in the nine-month geographic table. No sponsor, controlling holder or related-party financing is documented in the supplied text; that is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of absence. The view is bounded by what is not supplied: the merger agreements, the proxy statement, the indentures and credit agreements, and any source dated after August 6, 2026.

facts.label: Transaction summary and new debt issues
facts.text: The transaction that created the issuer closed on November 4, 2024: Treasure Holdco, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Berry Global Group, Inc., merged with Glatfelter Corporation, which concurrently changed its name to Magnera Corporation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "completed its merger (the “Transaction”) with the Glatfelter Corporation". The agreement is listed in the exhibit index as an RMT transaction agreement dated February 6, 2024 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:45] "2.1† RMT Transaction Agreement" (the agreement itself is not supplied; the label is the issuer's). Pre-transaction Treasure shareholders received shares representing 90 percent of the combined company and Glatfelter shareholders retained 10 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "pre-Transaction Treasure shareholders received shares of Magnera representing 90% of the combined company". Treasure was the accounting acquirer, so pre-closing history is the carve-out of the former parent's business and the Glatfelter business is consolidated from the closing date. The purchase consideration for the Glatfelter equity was recorded at 74, with goodwill of 36 on the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Fair value of GLT common stock concurrent with closing $ 74" and "Goodwill 36", and Glatfelter debt of 869 was assumed in the allocation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Debt (869 )". The Glatfelter contribution to FY2025 net sales was 1,145 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "The net sales for the year ended September 27, 2025 included $1,145 million from GLT." and unaudited pro forma FY2025 net sales and net loss including Glatfelter for the full year were 3,316 and (165) [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "unaudited pro forma net sales and net loss were $3,316 million and $(165) million".

facts.text: New debt raised at closing. The issuer consummated a 785 term loan due 2031, an 800 issuance of 7.25% first priority senior secured notes due 2031 and a 350 revolving credit facility [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "As part of the Transaction, the Company consummated a $785 million Term Loan due 2031". Use of proceeds: "The proceeds from the Term Loan and 7.25% Notes were used to retire a portion of GLT outstanding debt and fund a cash distribution to Berry." [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34]. The distribution to Berry was 1,111 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:25] "Cash distribution to Berry (1,111 ) — —", against proceeds from long-term borrowings of 1,556 in the cash flow statement, which is 29 below the 1,585 face amount of the term loan and notes (calc); the supplied text does not explain the 29. A prepayment penalty of 15 was charged for retiring debt concurrently with the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:16] "a $15 million prepayment penalty charge for retiring debt concurrently with the Transaction". The retained Glatfelter 4.75% first priority senior secured notes due October 2029 remain outstanding at 500 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "retained GLT 4.75 % First Priority Senior Secured Notes"; the indentures and a first supplemental indenture are exhibits but not supplied, so issuer and co-issuer entities, guarantors and collateral are not documented here beyond the names in the exhibit index [10-K_2025-09-27 page:46] "4.1 Indenture, by and between Treasure Escrow Corporation".

facts.label: Credit translations
facts.text: 1. Revenue durability. Evidence: no long-term arrangements with many customers [10-K_2025-09-27 page:8] "since we do not have long-term arrangements with many of our customers" and a top-ten share of about 42 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:27] "our top ten customers represented approximately 42% of net sales". Risk mechanic: short-tenor demand and concentrated accounts reduce revenue visibility; the filing's own statement that customers can shift suppliers quickly links competition to volume. Credit implication: debt service cannot lean on contracted revenue, so leverage tolerance should be lower than for contract-backed businesses, and monitoring should watch organic volume (negative at nine months) and any top-account loss. Counter: the consumer-oriented end markets are management's description of stability and the Americas volume rose 1 percent at nine months. 2. Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: input costs are polymer resin and pulps passed on with lag; a favourable price-cost spread of 11 in Q3 helped, while selling prices fell by 117 at nine months. Risk mechanic: in rising-cost periods the lag compresses margin and absorbs working capital (raw-material inventory rose in Q3, CP-1 shows free cash flow of (28) in Q3). Credit implication: cash conversion is the weak link in the near term; fourth-quarter delivery of the free cash flow guidance range is the monitoring point. Counter: management reports that Project CORE and synergy benefits are being realised [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:2] "realized benefits from Project CORE and merger synergies". 3. Geographic and currency risk. Evidence: Rest of World is about 45 percent of nine-month net sales, 58 percent of cash is outside the U.S. (CP-1) and unremitted foreign earnings were 336 at fiscal 2025 year end [10-K_2025-09-27 page:18] "Our unremitted foreign earnings were $336 million at the end of fiscal 2025." Risk mechanic: dollar debt is serviced from cash flows generated partly in euro, sterling and Brazilian real; repatriation is described by management as without significant restriction but the tax cost is not estimated. Credit implication: net debt that nets all cash overstates readily available liquidity at the U.S. borrower level, and translation moves reported leverage. Counter: the euro cross-currency swaps hedge part of the net investment. 4. Transaction and integration risk. Evidence: material weaknesses tied to the merger, reliance on legacy Berry IT under a transition services agreement, restructuring and integration charges recurring each quarter (CP-1). Risk mechanic: integration is incomplete and a former parent provides services; a failure of control or service continuity could delay reporting or disrupt order-to-cash. Credit implication: reporting reliability is a standing limitation and the monitoring posture should include remediation status at the FY2026 annual report. Counter: the auditor's opinion on the FY2025 financial statements was unqualified and management states there were no material errors. 5. Sponsor and shareholder alignment. Evidence: no sponsor, no dividends or buybacks through June 27, 2026, voluntary debt repayment. Risk mechanic: absent a controlling holder, distribution policy is set by a public-company board; the one large distribution (1,111) occurred at closing to the former parent. Credit implication: documented willingness points to deleveraging, but legal capacity to distribute, incur debt or prime depends on covenant baskets that are Not supplied, so no alignment conclusion beyond the documented actions is drawn. 6. Key uncertainties. The identity and rights of the holders of the 90 percent, the terms of the transition services agreement, the revolver's covenants and availability, the receivable programme size, and anything after August 6, 2026. Credit implication: each limits a committee view of control, liquidity or refinancing; none is treated as adverse by itself.

rows.label: Magnera is a two-segment specialty materials producer formed by the November 4, 2024 merger of a Berry carve-out with Glatfelter; new secured debt funded a 1,111 distribution to Berry. No sponsor; since closing it has repaid debt.

The top customer was about 14% and the top ten about 42% of FY2025 net sales, and many customers have no long-term arrangements.
The merger closed November 4, 2024 with a 785 term loan, 800 of 7.25% notes and a 350 revolver; 1,111 went to Berry and 500 of 4.75% notes stayed outstanding.
Material weaknesses persist and legacy IT still runs under a transition services agreement with Berry.
No dividends or buybacks appear through June 27, 2026 and 65 of debt was repaid, but holders and control rights are not disclosed.

facts.label: Credit view
facts.text: Magnera's creditors hold a leveraged but adequately liquid credit that is improving slowly and is not yet proven. Its strongest support is a long runway: the debt stack of USD 1,966 million has no maturity before October 2029, cash is USD 280 million, a USD 350 million revolver commitment is undrawn, and the issuer repaid USD 65 million in nine months without distributions. Its weakest point is the quality of the earnings and cash flow behind a 5.28x gross leverage figure: add-backs are USD 122 million of USD 372 million LTM adjusted EBITDA, operating income covers net interest only 0.42x, nine-month free cash flow was USD 32 million, and reporting controls are ineffective. The outcome turns on fourth-quarter cash delivery, on refinancing USD 500 million in 2029 and USD 1,466 million in 2031, and on revolver and covenant terms that are not yet visible.

facts.label: Key findings
facts.text: First, leverage is improving on filed figures but is sensitive to the earnings definition. Magnera's gross debt was USD 1,966 million at June 27, 2026 against LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 372 million, giving 5.28x gross and 4.53x net, down from 5.74x and 4.88x at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; basis CP-1 Chart data: leverage). The reduction came from higher LTM adjusted EBITDA and USD 65 million of repayments, with earnings contributing somewhat more. Operating income plus depreciation and amortization was USD 250 million LTM, so leverage would be 7.86x gross on that basis; add-backs of USD 122 million are about one third of adjusted EBITDA (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). The mechanism is that every quarter carries restructuring and integration add-backs, so creditors should treat the adjusted figure as the issuer's own measure and rely on the unadjusted figure for downside testing.

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: Strengths. A long maturity runway is the first strength: Magnera has no debt maturing before October 2029, and its term loan and notes carry no financial maintenance covenant (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities and covenants). Liquidity is the second: USD 280 million of cash and a USD 350 million undrawn revolver commitment total USD 630 million, with no facility expiring within twelve months (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity), though availability is unconfirmed. Deleveraging behaviour is the third: gross leverage fell from 5.74x to 5.28x, USD 65 million of debt was repaid in nine months and the equity statements show no dividends or buybacks (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: leverage and CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). Rate exposure is the fourth: USD 1,260 million, about 64%, of debt is fixed-rate notes, and the filing puts a quarter-point move in floating rates at about USD 2 million of annual interest (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the debt table; CP-1 Instruments). Operating scale and diversity are the fifth: 45 manufacturing facilities across two segments and consumer-oriented end markets, with the Americas earning a higher margin (Documentary Fact and Management Language for the stability description; CP-1A Company and operating model).

Thesis: a long-dated secured debt stack with ample near-term liquidity and falling leverage supports Magnera's creditors, but thin cash conversion, heavy add-backs, customer concentration and unremediated reporting controls leave the credit reliant on fiscal 2026 cash delivery and on refinancing in 2029 and 2031
Claims outside debt, maximum of stated amounts

Revolver borrowing base, letters of credit, availability and covenants not supplied
Executed term loan agreement, indentures and guarantor list not supplied
Interim cash interest and cash taxes not supplied (annual cash taxes of USD 22 million and annual cash interest of USD 124 million are supplied for FY2025)
Ownership, control rights and transition services terms not supplied
Add-back bridge by line not supplied (category totals only)
Prior-year comparatives are carve-out and part-period
No ratings or market pricing supplied

facts.label: Evidence trace view
facts.text: Magnera's analysis is traceable enough to support a view of its current debt, liquidity and earnings, and not yet a view of revolver access, covenant headroom or creditor legal capacity. Every citation quotation checked sits on the page it names, every derived figure recomputed from the filings equals the handoff, and unsupported claims are labelled as gaps rather than filled. ### Read-through: evidence, source risk, consequence

Debt capacity evidence. The latest debt note lists four instruments and a footing total, and states that the term loan and secured notes carry no financial maintenance covenants: [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:9] "Despite not having financial maintenance covenants on our term loan and secured notes". The source risk is that the revolver is described separately as an asset-based facility with no borrowings, yet its covenant, availability and letter of credit terms are not printed anywhere in the pack. The consequence is that downstream liquidity can use cash and the stated revolver size but must present undrawn capacity as unconfirmed, and must not state that no covenant applies to the revolver. The compliance statement covers "all long-term debt covenants": [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:9] "We are in compliance with all long-term debt covenants as of June 27, 2026."

Refinancing evidence. Management says it intends to refinance, and the annual report states there are no maturities before 2029: [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "The Company has no future maturities of long-term debt until 2029, at which point $500 million and $1,531 million are due in fiscal year 2029 and 2031, respectively". The latest interim report repeats the intention: [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "which we intend to refinance prior to maturity". Source risk: the maturity schedule is printed only in the annual report and as of September 27, 2025; interim notes give maturity dates but no schedule, and no source after August 6, 2026 can show a refinancing. Consequence: the maturity wall for the cutoff must be rebuilt from the interim debt table and labelled as derived, and any refinancing between August 6, 2026 and the cutoff is unknown.

Reporting reliability evidence. The annual audit has an unqualified opinion on the statements and an adverse opinion on internal control: [10-K_2025-09-27 page:20] "expressed an adverse opinion thereon". The latest interim report says: [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:20] "management has concluded that our disclosure controls and procedures were not effective as of the last day of the period covered by this report". Source risk: unaudited interim figures rest on controls the issuer itself calls ineffective, tied to merger accounting and legacy IT systems. Consequence: downstream modules should treat interim figures as filed but carry the control weakness as a standing limitation, and CP-5 should test interim totals against the printed foots.

Comparability evidence. Year-to-date FY2026 against prior year includes merger revenue in the comparison base: [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:17] "The net sales increase included revenue from the prior year merger of $112 million". Source risk: the prior-year interim and the FY2024 columns are carve-out or partial-period figures, so growth rates mix organic change, acquisition and currency. Consequence: CP-1 must not present unadjusted year-on-year growth as organic, and should use the releases' comparable-basis tables only as attributed management measures.

Off-balance sheet evidence. Receivables are sold under customer programmes: [10-K_2025-09-27 page:27] "The Company participates in customer supply chain financing programs to collect certain receivables through third-party financial institutions." Source risk: no volume or balance is printed in any source. Consequence: operating cash flow and working capital cannot be adjusted for the programme, and CP-2 must show it as an unquantified item. Other claims outside the debt table that are located: unfunded frozen pension plans [10-K_2025-09-27 page:39] "all of which are frozen to new participants and existing participants from accruing additional benefits and are unfunded"; Fox River environmental liability [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:12] "outstanding balance of the environmental liability and corresponding escrow asset were $17 million and $9 million"; Brazilian tax claims [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:12] "not expected to exceed $66 million as of June 27, 2026"; operating leases [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:8] with finance leases described as not material in the annual report.

Perimeter evidence. The annual report presents one consolidated entity and the exhibit index names a separate borrower entity and an unsupplied guarantor list. Source risk: restricted and unrestricted group, guarantor coverage and structural subordination of the notes cannot be mapped. Consequence: CP-2 should not assert guarantor coverage or collateral scope beyond the instrument names.

Next evidence action: retrieve the term loan agreement, the asset-based revolving credit agreement and its amendment, the three indentures and the guarantor list (all exhibits named in the annual report index), plus any filing, release or report dated after August 6, 2026 up to the cutoff, before liquidity, covenant or refinancing conclusions are finalised.
## Calculations
These are footing and consistency checks on printed figures, to test source integrity. They do not normalise or reconcile figures to a model. All amounts are USD millions.

## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| On filed figures, Magnera's leverage at June 27, 2026 was 5.28x gross and 4.53x net on LTM adjusted EBITDA, down from FY2025. Interest cover is 2.91x on a cash-interest proxy and free cash flow is thin. | Medium | Adjusted EBITDA is a company measure with large add-backs, interim cash interest is not reported, and revolver availability and covenants are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Gross debt was 1,966 and cash 280 at June 27, 2026, against LTM adjusted EBITDA of 372. | Leverage fell from 5.74x gross at FY2025 to 5.28x, from higher LTM EBITDA and 65 of debt repayments. | High |

| Operating income plus depreciation and amortization was 250 LTM, versus 372 adjusted. | On unadjusted earnings, gross leverage is 7.86x; add-backs of 122 carry a third of the adjusted figure. | Medium |

| LTM net interest expense was 151 against operating income of 63, and every period shows a net loss. | Earnings do not cover interest after depreciation; cover of 2.91x depends on adjusted EBITDA. | Medium |

| Nine-month free cash flow was 32 against fiscal 2026 guidance of 90 to 110, and the third quarter was negative. | Delivering guidance needs 58 to 78 in the fourth quarter; working capital absorbed cash in the third quarter. | Medium |

| No debt matures before October 2029 and cash plus the 350 revolver commitment totals 630, but availability is unconfirmed. | Runway is long, yet 500 falls due in 2029 and 1,466 in 2031, and borrowing base and letters of credit are unknown. | Medium |
### Financial base view

The filed statements support a reliable financial base for Magnera Corporation, one consolidated entity, in USD millions across four balance-sheet dates (September 27, 2025, December 27, 2025, March 28, 2026 and June 27, 2026) and the flow periods FY2025, each FY2026 quarter, the nine months to June 27, 2026 and the matching nine months of FY2025. Every total and reconciliation tested foots to the filed statement, and the by-function expense block reconciles to operating income in each tested period (see Calculations). The base is limited, not blocked: earnings are measured on the company's adjusted EBITDA, which carries add-backs of about one third of the adjusted figure on an LTM basis; prior-year comparatives are carve-out and part-period (the Glatfelter business is consolidated only from November 4, 2024); interim cash interest and cash taxes are not reported, so cover uses a labelled proxy that ties exactly to the one reported annual cash interest figure; and the revolver is known only by size, maturity and a no-borrowings statement. Leverage and cover use gross debt principal as printed before the discount line and LTM adjusted EBITDA built from filed figures. No guidance, pro forma or synergy-adjusted release figure enters any ratio.

### Interpretation: evidence, risk mechanism, credit implication

Leverage. Evidence: gross debt principal fell from 2,031 at September 27, 2025 to 1,966 at June 27, 2026 through repayments of the term loan (731 to 706) and the 7.25% notes (800 to 760) [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:8] "7.25% First Priority Senior Secured Notes November 2031 760 800", while LTM adjusted EBITDA rose from 354 to 372. Risk mechanism: both legs help, but the EBITDA is a company-defined measure and the gap to operating income plus D&A is 122 LTM. Credit implication: filed-basis leverage of 5.28x gross and 4.53x net is improving but remains above five times gross for a business that reports a net loss in every period shown. Higher LTM EBITDA contributed somewhat more of the improvement than debt repayment (calc: EBITDA change alone gives 5.46, debt change alone 5.55; see Calculations).

Add-backs and definition risk. Evidence: segment notes reconcile adjusted EBITDA to operating income through restructuring and integration charges, Argentina hyperinflation, carve-out allocation and other non-cash charges; the LTM restructuring and other activities charge was 81, and the nine-month charge of 61 splits into severance 13, facility exit 3, non-cash 10 and integration and other 35 [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:7] "Charges 13 3 10 35 61". The 10-K sized only the Project CORE capacity rationalisation at about 20 over two years [10-K_2025-09-27 page:15] "these actions are projected to cost approximately $20 million"; the charge line is therefore broader than that programme, and the integration and other component recurs each quarter, with a further 23 in Q3 including a loss on sale of a facility. Risk mechanism: add-backs that recur every quarter blur the line between non-recurring and operating cost; lenders and rating methodologies may haircut them. Credit implication: committee leverage should be shown on both bases (5.28x and 7.86x gross), and a covenant-style EBITDA cannot be inferred because no definition from an executed agreement is supplied.

Interest cover. Evidence: net interest expense was 151 LTM against operating income of 63, so operating income covers interest 0.42 times; adjusted EBITDA covers the cash-interest proxy 2.91 times and net interest 2.46 times. Risk mechanism: floating-rate term loan exposure (the filing says a change of 0.25 percent changes annual interest expense by about 2) [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "A change of 0.25% on these floating interest rate exposures would increase our annual interest expense by approximately $2 million." Credit implication: cover is adequate only on the adjusted measure; lower SOFR (about 3.62 percent at June 27, 2026 against about 4.19 percent at September 27, 2025 per the filings) has helped the floating portion.

Cash flow and liquidity. Evidence: nine-month cash from operations was 76 and capex 44, so free cash flow was 32, up from (45) in 9M FY2025. Quarterly free cash flow was (13) in Q1, 73 in Q2 and (28) in Q3 (calc); working capital changes absorbed 54 in Q3 (calc: (34) cumulative against 20 at six months). Management guides fiscal 2026 free cash flow of 90 to 110, which needs 58 to 78 in the fourth quarter. Risk mechanism: large quarterly swings from working capital and raw-material inflation (raw materials inventory rose from 175 to 201 in the quarter); customer receivable programmes are off balance sheet and unquantified. Credit implication: debt reduction depends on a strong fourth quarter; liquidity is 280 of cash plus a 350 undrawn revolver commitment, but the revolver's availability, borrowing base and any covenant are not supplied and 58 percent of cash is outside the U.S. [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "of which approximately 58% is located outside the U.S."

Maturities and refinancing. Evidence: no maturity before October 2029; 500 falls due then and 1,466 in November 2031; management says it intends to refinance prior to maturity [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "which we intend to refinance prior to maturity". The book value of marketable debt exceeded fair value by 48 at June 27, 2026, against 136 at March 28, 2026, which is a narrower discount in the latest quarter [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:10] "The book value of our marketable long-term indebtedness exceeded fair value by $48 million as of June 27, 2026." Credit implication: runway is long, but two instruments mature within weeks of each other in 2029 (notes in October, revolver in November) and the 2031 stack is large; any springing maturity in the revolver is unknown.

Earnings quality. Evidence: Q3 adjusted EBITDA rose from 91 to 99 on a price-cost spread gain of 11 [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:15] "The operating income increase included a favorable price cost spread of $11 million", while net sales rose from 839 to 857 including favorable currency of 21 and a selling price decrease of 8. Rest of World adjusted EBITDA fell from 30 to 28 while Americas rose from 61 to 71. Risk mechanism: the Q3 gain is concentrated in one region and in price-cost timing during raw-material inflation; management says it is holding to the lower end of its adjusted EBITDA guidance range [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:1] "while holding to the lower end of our adjusted EBITDA guidance range". Credit implication: treat the 372 LTM base as not yet showing a clean upward trend, and note that the low end of the 380 to 410 range implies a fourth quarter of 98 against 90 a year earlier (calc).

spans.text: ## Request

Issuer: Magnera Corp (issuer id magn), NYSE ticker MAGN; registrant name in the filings "Magnera Corporation" (formerly Glatfelter Corporation). As-of date and cutoff: 2026-11-05. Pathway: credit_snapshot. Reporting currency USD; the filings report in USD millions. Current period per the context: Q3 FY2026, the quarterly period ended June 27, 2026, with the nine months to that date; prior period: FY2025, the fiscal year ended September 27, 2025.

Task: the business and transaction fact pack a committee reads first, from a creditor perspective. It covers company and operating model, company profile, transaction and new debt issues, ownership, issuer-level governance behaviour, a dated timeline, logged conflicts, credit translations (evidence, risk mechanic, credit implication) and the readiness of the downstream consumers. ### Business and transaction view

The supplied sources show a mid-sized, publicly listed manufacturer of nonwoven and film-based specialty materials for consumer-oriented end markets, formed in a combination in which a carve-out of the former parent's health, hygiene and specialties business merged with Glatfelter. The structure matters to a creditor in three ways. First, the combination was financed with new first priority secured debt and a cash distribution to the former parent, so opening leverage was set by the transaction rather than by operations; since closing the documented capital allocation is voluntary debt repayment, with no dividends or buybacks in the equity statements. Second, the integration is incomplete: the issuer reports material weaknesses tied to the merger and still depends on the former parent's legacy IT systems under a transition services agreement, so the reporting base is exposed to a counterparty that is also the former owner. Third, the operating model combines high input-cost pass-through with lag, a large customer concentration (top ten about 42 percent of FY2025 net sales) and a geographic mix in which Rest of World, the lower-margin segment, is the largest region in the nine-month geographic table. No sponsor, controlling holder or related-party financing is documented in the supplied text; that is a gap in the evidence, not a finding of absence. The view is bounded by what is not supplied: the merger agreements, the proxy statement, the indentures and credit agreements, and any source dated after August 6, 2026.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

The transaction that created the issuer closed on November 4, 2024: Treasure Holdco, Inc., a wholly owned subsidiary of Berry Global Group, Inc., merged with Glatfelter Corporation, which concurrently changed its name to Magnera Corporation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "completed its merger (the “Transaction”) with the Glatfelter Corporation". The agreement is listed in the exhibit index as an RMT transaction agreement dated February 6, 2024 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:45] "2.1† RMT Transaction Agreement" (the agreement itself is not supplied; the label is the issuer's). Pre-transaction Treasure shareholders received shares representing 90 percent of the combined company and Glatfelter shareholders retained 10 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "pre-Transaction Treasure shareholders received shares of Magnera representing 90% of the combined company". Treasure was the accounting acquirer, so pre-closing history is the carve-out of the former parent's business and the Glatfelter business is consolidated from the closing date. The purchase consideration for the Glatfelter equity was recorded at 74, with goodwill of 36 on the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Fair value of GLT common stock concurrent with closing $ 74" and "Goodwill 36", and Glatfelter debt of 869 was assumed in the allocation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "Debt (869 )". The Glatfelter contribution to FY2025 net sales was 1,145 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "The net sales for the year ended September 27, 2025 included $1,145 million from GLT." and unaudited pro forma FY2025 net sales and net loss including Glatfelter for the full year were 3,316 and (165) [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "unaudited pro forma net sales and net loss were $3,316 million and $(165) million".

New debt raised at closing. The issuer consummated a 785 term loan due 2031, an 800 issuance of 7.25% first priority senior secured notes due 2031 and a 350 revolving credit facility [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "As part of the Transaction, the Company consummated a $785 million Term Loan due 2031". Use of proceeds: "The proceeds from the Term Loan and 7.25% Notes were used to retire a portion of GLT outstanding debt and fund a cash distribution to Berry." [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34]. The distribution to Berry was 1,111 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:25] "Cash distribution to Berry (1,111 ) — —", against proceeds from long-term borrowings of 1,556 in the cash flow statement, which is 29 below the 1,585 face amount of the term loan and notes (calc); the supplied text does not explain the 29. Berry also transferred its health, hygiene and specialties global nonwovens and films business to Treasure as part of the closing [10-K_2025-09-27 page:26] "Berry received a cash distribution and, in turn, transferred". A prepayment penalty of 15 was charged for retiring debt concurrently with the transaction [10-K_2025-09-27 page:16] "a $15 million prepayment penalty charge for retiring debt concurrently with the Transaction". The retained Glatfelter 4.75% first priority senior secured notes due October 2029 remain outstanding at 500 [10-K_2025-09-27 page:34] "retained GLT 4.75 % First Priority Senior Secured Notes"; the indentures and a first supplemental indenture are exhibits but not supplied, so issuer and co-issuer entities, guarantors and collateral are not documented here beyond the names in the exhibit index [10-K_2025-09-27 page:46] "4.1 Indenture, by and between Treasure Escrow Corporation".

Liquidity and status. The transaction brought cash of 37 into the group (acquired cash), and cash was 305 at September 27, 2025 and 280 at June 27, 2026 (CP-1). The transaction is complete; the 10-K presents the final allocation [10-K_2025-09-27 page:32] "The following table summarizes the final purchase price allocation:" and describes the measurement period adjustments. There was no new debt issuance in the first nine months of FY2026; the only financing flows are repayments of 65. Subsequent events: no new issuance or refinancing is reported in any supplied source dated after the closing, and nothing is supplied after August 6, 2026. Management says it intends to refinance long-term debt prior to maturity [10-Q_2026-06-27 page:19] "which we intend to refinance prior to maturity"; no refinancing is documented. Management's pro forma adjusted EBITDA includes a synergy add-on that fell across the three releases: [EX-99.1_2026-02-05 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 60", [EX-99.1_2026-05-07 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 48" and [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:6] "Synergies and cost reductions 35". These are attributed management figures, not filed results. The pro forma total moved from 423 to 412 to 405 [EX-99.1_2026-02-05 page:6] "Comparable Adjusted EBITDA (1)(6) $ 423", [EX-99.1_2026-05-07 page:6] "PF Adjusted EBITDA $ 412" and [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:6] "PF Adjusted EBITDA $ 405", while the filed LTM adjusted EBITDA built in CP-1 rose from 363 to 364 to 372; the direction of the two series differs because the synergy add-on shrank faster than LTM earnings grew. Whether the shrinking add-on reflects realisation of synergies in reported results is Analyst Interpretation and is not stated by the issuer.

| Subject | Span one | Span two | Downstream effect |

| Facility count | [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "Our Americas operations consist of 22 manufacturing facilities" and [10-K_2025-09-27 page:5] "Our Rest of World operations consist of 23 manufacturing facilities" (45 in total, calc) | [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:2] "Operating across 44 global facilities" | The counts differ by one at different dates and sources; the supplied text does not say whether the difference is a sale, a closure or a definition. Not reconciled; capacity statements should cite the source and date |

| Record quarter claim | [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:1] "We delivered a record third quarter led by organic volume growth" | Filed quarterly adjusted EBITDA in the supplied sources: 84, 89, 91, 90 (derived), 93, 90 and 99 across seven quarters | The claim is consistent with the seven quarters in the pack (99 is the highest) but cannot be tested beyond them; treat as Management Language. Not a conflict of figures |

| Cash taxes | CP-0 and CP-1 listed cash taxes as Not supplied | [10-K_2025-09-27 page:37] "The Company paid cash taxes of $22 million, $9 million, and $29 million in fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023" | Annual cash taxes are printed; interim cash taxes remain Not supplied (see consistency section) |
### Credit translations

1. Revenue durability. Evidence: no long-term arrangements with many customers [10-K_2025-09-27 page:8] "since we do not have long-term arrangements with many of our customers" and a top-ten share of about 42 percent [10-K_2025-09-27 page:27] "our top ten customers represented approximately 42% of net sales". Risk mechanic: short-tenor demand and concentrated accounts reduce revenue visibility; the filing's own statement that customers can shift suppliers quickly links competition to volume. Credit implication: debt service cannot lean on contracted revenue, so leverage tolerance should be lower than for contract-backed businesses, and monitoring should watch organic volume (negative at nine months) and any top-account loss. Counter: the consumer-oriented end markets are management's description of stability and the Americas volume rose 1 percent at nine months.

2. Margin and cash-flow risk. Evidence: input costs are polymer resin and pulps passed on with lag; a favourable price-cost spread of 11 in Q3 helped, while selling prices fell by 117 at nine months. Risk mechanic: in rising-cost periods the lag compresses margin and absorbs working capital (raw-material inventory rose in Q3, CP-1 shows free cash flow of (28) in Q3). Credit implication: cash conversion is the weak link in the near term; fourth-quarter delivery of the free cash flow guidance range is the monitoring point. Counter: management reports that Project CORE and synergy benefits are being realised [EX-99.1_2026-08-06 page:2] "realized benefits from Project CORE and merger synergies".

3. Geographic and currency risk. Evidence: Rest of World is about 45 percent of nine-month net sales, 58 percent of cash is outside the U.S. (CP-1) and unremitted foreign earnings were 336 at fiscal 2025 year end [10-K_2025-09-27 page:18] "Our unremitted foreign earnings were $336 million at the end of fiscal 2025." Risk mechanic: dollar debt is serviced from cash flows generated partly in euro, sterling and Brazilian real; repatriation is described by management as without significant restriction but the tax cost is not estimated. Credit implication: net debt that nets all cash overstates readily available liquidity at the U.S. borrower level, and translation moves reported leverage. Counter: the euro cross-currency swaps hedge part of the net investment.

4. Transaction and integration risk. Evidence: material weaknesses tied to the merger, reliance on legacy Berry IT under a transition services agreement, restructuring and integration charges recurring each quarter (CP-1). Risk mechanic: integration is incomplete and a former parent provides services; a failure of control or service continuity could delay reporting or disrupt order-to-cash. Credit implication: reporting reliability is a standing limitation and the monitoring posture should include remediation status at the FY2026 annual report. Counter: the auditor's opinion on the FY2025 financial statements was unqualified and management states there were no material errors.

5. Sponsor and shareholder alignment. Evidence: no sponsor, no dividends or buybacks through June 27, 2026, voluntary debt repayment. Risk mechanic: absent a controlling holder, distribution policy is set by a public-company board; the one large distribution (1,111) occurred at closing to the former parent. Credit implication: documented willingness points to deleveraging, but legal capacity to distribute, incur debt or prime depends on covenant baskets that are Not supplied, so no alignment conclusion beyond the documented actions is drawn.

6. Key uncertainties. The identity and rights of the holders of the 90 percent, the terms of the transition services agreement, the revolver's covenants and availability, the receivable programme size, and anything after August 6, 2026. Credit implication: each limits a committee view of control, liquidity or refinancing; none is treated as adverse by itself.
### Consumer readiness

| CP-2 fundamental credit synthesis | READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS | The operating model table, the customer and pass-through mechanics, the transaction structure, the governance observations and the credit translations | Links earnings durability and structure to the leverage and liquidity in the financial base | Ownership, control rights, legal capacity, transition services terms and executed debt documents are Not supplied; CP-2 must not assert covenant or guarantor protections |

| Maintenance versus growth capex split | Free cash flow quality | Low |
### Consistency with upstream handoffs
- CP-1 is consistent with this handoff on debt, cash, earnings and guidance figures; the facility count and ownership items here are new.

- Correction to CP-0 and CP-1: both handoffs listed cash taxes paid as Not supplied after searching "income taxes paid" and "cash paid for". The annual report does print annual cash taxes: [10-K_2025-09-27 page:37] "The Company paid cash taxes of $22 million, $9 million, and $29 million in fiscal years 2025, 2024, and 2023". Annual FY2025 cash taxes of 22 are therefore supplied; interim cash taxes remain Not supplied (a search for "cash taxes" finds only this sentence). The earlier handoffs cannot be edited; downstream modules should use the annual figure with this label.

- CP-0 said ownership percentages and control rights were not supplied; confirmed. This handoff records the 90 and 10 percent split at closing as a documented fact and keeps current holders as Insufficient Information.

spans.text: ## Request

Magnera Corp (issuer id magn), as of 2026-11-05, pathway credit_snapshot: this module synthesises the fundamental credit view from the CP-1 financial base and the CP-1A business and transaction fact pack, in USD, for the quarter ended June 27, 2026 against fiscal 2025. Scope is upstream evidence only, with no peer ranking, instrument recommendation or recovery conclusion.
## Sources

Issuer sources behind the upstream handoffs (exact pinned names and sha256). This module reopens no source text and quotes nothing; each source is relied on only through the CP-1 and CP-1A handoffs, which carry the locators.
| Source (exact name) | sha256 |
| 10-Q_2026-06-27_form10q.htm.jsonl | 9bf0a737948e12b9a435299f2c1d5be9f80cbb7bbc87ba8bb4baa3f7134d16c0 |
Context (user settings, not issuer evidence): context, sha256 4a094c245ff44dd6e34e569a37f728533980efba9932af440a0d9b2f6b50325a.
Supplied handoffs:
| Module | sha256 | Use |
| CP-0 | a8b15cc07abfbb855ac56418114ac7639ccb07ec7eb0a78b02caf33e517da591 | Source readiness and limits |
| CP-1 | a78bacbb4723d5e8436e6fd7e6e91834e21d1b667c43041d9840bc2ad8acdf4e | Financial base: leverage, cover, liquidity, maturities, claims outside debt, guidance |
| CP-1A | dc1cfc41f7ccf460c47df520b4e07d54a6ff2eeaeab479e0167f855b94cb0f46 | Business and transaction: operating model, profile, transaction, governance behaviour, credit translations |
Basis labels used below name the CP-1 or CP-1A section and row, for example "CP-1 Chart data: leverage" or "CP-1A Company and operating model, Customers".
## Findings
### Reader summary
| Bottom line | Confidence | Main limitation |

| Magnera's creditors hold a leveraged but liquid credit: gross debt is 5.28x LTM adjusted EBITDA, nothing matures before October 2029, and debt is being repaid. Thin cash conversion, heavy add-backs and weak reporting controls keep the view cautious. | Medium | Revolver availability and covenants, executed debt documents, ownership terms and anything after August 6, 2026 are not supplied. |
| Finding | Creditor impact | Confidence |

| Gross leverage was 5.28x and net leverage 4.53x at June 27, 2026, but 7.86x gross on earnings before add-backs. | Headline leverage is improving; one third of adjusted EBITDA rests on management add-backs. | Medium |

| Cash was USD 280 million with a USD 350 million undrawn revolver commitment, and USD 500 million falls due in 2029 and USD 1,466 million in 2031. | Near-term liquidity looks adequate and the runway is long, but 2029 and 2031 need refinancing and availability is unconfirmed. | Medium |

| Nine-month free cash flow was USD 32 million against guidance of USD 90 million to USD 110 million, and the third quarter was negative. | Debt reduction depends on a strong fourth quarter; working capital swings with raw-material costs. | Medium |

| The top ten customers were about 42% of FY2025 net sales and many have no long-term arrangements. | Short-tenor, concentrated demand gives low revenue visibility and exposes margins to lagged cost pass-through. | Medium |

| Material weaknesses persist and no dividends or buybacks appear while debt is repaid. | Reporting risk is elevated; documented behaviour supports deleveraging but legal capacity is untested. | Medium |
### Credit view

Magnera's creditors hold a leveraged but adequately liquid credit that is improving slowly and is not yet proven. Its strongest support is a long runway: the debt stack of USD 1,966 million has no maturity before October 2029, cash is USD 280 million, a USD 350 million revolver commitment is undrawn, and the issuer repaid USD 65 million in nine months without distributions. Its weakest point is the quality of the earnings and cash flow behind a 5.28x gross leverage figure: add-backs are USD 122 million of USD 372 million LTM adjusted EBITDA, operating income covers net interest only 0.42x, nine-month free cash flow was USD 32 million, and reporting controls are ineffective. The outcome turns on fourth-quarter cash delivery, on refinancing USD 500 million in 2029 and USD 1,466 million in 2031, and on revolver and covenant terms that are not yet visible.
### Credit assessment
| Assessment | Category | Confidence | Basis |

| Fundamental credit view: leveraged industrial credit with adequate near-term liquidity, a long maturity runway, improving but add-back-dependent earnings and thin cash conversion; financial risk is weighed above business risk | Analyst Interpretation | Medium (below High because CP-1A records READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS for CP-2 and CP-1 notes unconfirmed revolver availability) | CP-1 Chart data: leverage, liquidity, debt maturities; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics; CP-1A Company and operating model; CP-1A Credit translations |

| Thesis: a long-dated secured debt stack with ample near-term liquidity and falling leverage supports Magnera's creditors, but thin cash conversion, heavy add-backs, customer concentration and unremediated reporting controls leave the credit reliant on fiscal 2026 cash delivery and on refinancing in 2029 and 2031 | Analyst Interpretation | Medium | As above |
### Key findings

First, leverage is improving on filed figures but is sensitive to the earnings definition. Magnera's gross debt was USD 1,966 million at June 27, 2026 against LTM adjusted EBITDA of USD 372 million, giving 5.28x gross and 4.53x net, down from 5.74x and 4.88x at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; basis CP-1 Chart data: leverage). The reduction came from higher LTM adjusted EBITDA and USD 65 million of repayments, with earnings contributing somewhat more. Operating income plus depreciation and amortization was USD 250 million LTM, so leverage would be 7.86x gross on that basis; add-backs of USD 122 million are about one third of adjusted EBITDA (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). The mechanism is that every quarter carries restructuring and integration add-backs, so creditors should treat the adjusted figure as the issuer's own measure and rely on the unadjusted figure for downside testing.

Second, coverage is adequate only on the adjusted measure. Magnera's LTM adjusted EBITDA covers a cash-interest proxy 2.91x, but LTM operating income of USD 63 million covers net interest expense of USD 151 million only 0.42x, and the issuer reported a net loss in every period shown, USD 112 million LTM (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1 Chart data: interest cover). The cash-interest figure for interim periods is a proxy, not a reported amount. The implication is that interest is paid from depreciation and non-cash charges rather than from operating profit, so any EBITDA shortfall reaches liquidity quickly.

Third, cash conversion is the weak link in the near term. Magnera generated USD 32 million of free cash flow in nine months of fiscal 2026 and a negative USD 28 million in the third quarter, as working capital absorbed USD 54 million (calculated by difference in CP-1). Management guides to USD 90 million to USD 110 million for the year, which requires USD 58 million to USD 78 million in the fourth quarter (Management Language for the guidance; Analyst Interpretation for the requirement). Raw-material inventory rose in the third quarter and the price-cost spread helped earnings, so cash and margin both depend on how fast cost changes pass through (CP-1A Company and operating model, Pricing and pass-through). The implication is that deleveraging pace in the next two quarters is a function of working capital release, not of earnings growth.

Fourth, liquidity and maturities favour creditors, with one unverified element. Magnera had USD 280 million of cash, about 58% of it outside the U.S., plus a USD 350 million asset-based revolver commitment with no borrowings, a combined USD 630 million before any borrowing base or letters of credit (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity). The revolver's availability, drawn letters of credit and covenants are Not supplied (Insufficient Information). The term loan and the notes carry no financial maintenance covenant, which lowers the chance of a covenant-driven default (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Instruments, liquidity build and covenants). The implication is that near-term default risk is low on the information supplied, and the question moves to refinancing.

Fifth, refinancing risk is concentrated. The 4.75% notes of USD 500 million mature in October 2029, the revolver in November 2029, and the term loan of USD 706 million and 7.25% notes of USD 760 million in November 2031 (CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities). A quarter of debt falls due in 2029 and three quarters in 2031 (calc). Management says it intends to refinance prior to maturity, and the fair value of the debt sat USD 48 million below book at June 27, 2026 against USD 136 million at March 28, 2026 (CP-1 Interpretation). The mechanism is that a weak operating year in fiscal 2027 or 2028 would meet the 2029 maturity wall with leverage still above five times gross, narrowing refinancing options; the implication is a monitoring posture focused on deleveraging progress and market access ahead of 2028.

Sixth, the business gives limited revenue visibility. The top ten customers were about 42% of FY2025 net sales, the largest about 14%, and many customers have no long-term arrangements (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Company and operating model, Customers and Contract tenor). Organic volume fell 1% in nine months while currency and the merger lifted reported sales (CP-1A Volume and price drivers). The implication is that revenue can move quickly with account decisions, so creditors rely on cost pass-through and the Americas segment, which earns about two thirds of adjusted EBITDA, rather than on contracted revenue.

Seventh, reporting reliability and related-party dependence are open items. Material weaknesses and ineffective disclosure controls persist at June 27, 2026, and legacy IT still runs under a transition services agreement with the former parent (Documentary Fact; CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). The implication is that interim figures carry control risk and that remediation status at the fiscal 2026 annual report is a monitoring trigger; the terms of the agreement are Not supplied.
### Strengths and weaknesses

Strengths. A long maturity runway is the first strength: Magnera has no debt maturing before October 2029, and its term loan and notes carry no financial maintenance covenant (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities and covenants). Liquidity is the second: USD 280 million of cash and a USD 350 million undrawn revolver commitment total USD 630 million, with no facility expiring within twelve months (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: liquidity), though availability is unconfirmed. Deleveraging behaviour is the third: gross leverage fell from 5.74x to 5.28x, USD 65 million of debt was repaid in nine months and the equity statements show no dividends or buybacks (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Chart data: leverage and CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour). Rate exposure is the fourth: USD 1,260 million, about 64%, of debt is fixed-rate notes, and the filing puts a quarter-point move in floating rates at about USD 2 million of annual interest (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the debt table; CP-1 Instruments). Operating scale and diversity are the fifth: 45 manufacturing facilities across two segments and consumer-oriented end markets, with the Americas earning a higher margin (Documentary Fact and Management Language for the stability description; CP-1A Company and operating model).

Weaknesses. Earnings quality is the first weakness: add-backs of USD 122 million LTM, recurring restructuring and integration charges, and unadjusted leverage of 7.86x gross (Analyst Interpretation; CP-1 Financials and credit metrics). Interest burden is the second: net interest expense of USD 151 million LTM against operating income of USD 63 million and a net loss every period (Documentary Fact and calculation; CP-1). Cash flow is the third: free cash flow of USD 32 million for nine months against guidance requiring a strong fourth quarter, and unquantified receivable programmes that sit outside reported debt (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure). Customer concentration and short contract tenor are the fourth (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). Reporting controls and dependence on the former parent's systems are the fifth (Documentary Fact; CP-1A). Claims outside debt are the sixth: operating leases of USD 60 million, a cross-currency swap liability of USD 78 million, Brazilian tax claims of up to USD 66 million, an environmental liability of USD 17 million against a USD 9 million escrow asset and an unfunded pension obligation of USD 27 million at September 27, 2025 (Documentary Fact; CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure; treating all as debt would lift gross leverage to about 5.95x, calc). Equity quality is the seventh: book equity of USD 1,017 million is mostly goodwill and intangibles of USD 858 million, leaving tangible equity of about USD 159 million (Analyst Interpretation, calculated from the balance sheet in CP-1).
### Key credit risks
| Risk | Mechanic | Credit implication | Severity | Basis |

| Refinancing concentration in 2029 and 2031 | USD 500 million of notes in October 2029 and a revolver in November 2029, then USD 1,466 million in November 2031; leverage still above five times gross | Refinancing cost and access depend on deleveraging and earnings quality over fiscal 2027 and 2028; a weak year narrows options | Material | CP-1 Chart data: debt maturities and leverage |

| Cash conversion below guidance | Nine-month free cash flow of USD 32 million; working capital absorbed USD 54 million in the third quarter; raw-material inventory rising | A shortfall slows repayment and leaves leverage near current levels into year end | Material | CP-1 Financials and credit metrics; CP-1A Company and operating model |

| Earnings quality and add-back dependence | Add-backs of USD 122 million LTM recur each quarter; unadjusted leverage 7.86x gross | A lender definition of EBITDA may be lower than the issuer's; covenant-style headroom cannot be assessed | Material | CP-1 Financials and credit metrics |

| Liquidity access unverified | Revolver size known but borrowing base, letters of credit and covenants Not supplied; 58% of cash outside the U.S. | Usable liquidity may be lower than USD 630 million; trapped or taxed cash would reduce U.S. debt-service capacity | Material | CP-1 Chart data: liquidity; CP-0 gaps |

| Customer concentration and short tenor | Top ten customers about 42% of FY2025 net sales; many customers lack long-term arrangements; lagged pass-through | Account loss or repricing reaches revenue and margin quickly | Material | CP-1A Company and operating model |

| Reporting controls and former-parent dependence | Material weaknesses; legacy IT under a transition services agreement; ineffective disclosure controls | Reporting delay or error risk; continuity risk if services end; reporting-covenant terms unknown | Material | CP-1A Ownership and issuer-level governance behaviour |

| Rates and currency | USD 706 million floating term loan; dollar debt against euro, sterling, real and peso earnings | Rate moves change interest cost modestly; currency moves change reported leverage and the value of offshore cash | Minor | CP-1 Instruments; CP-1A Currency exposure |

| Claims outside debt | Leases, swap liability, Brazilian tax claims, environmental and pension obligations | Add to fixed claims on cash flow outside the leverage ratios | Minor | CP-1 Claims outside the debt figure |

No risk is rated Critical: no covenant breach, maturity within twelve months or liquidity shortfall is shown by the supplied evidence, which is not a finding that none exists in the unsupplied documents.
## Calculations
All amounts USD millions unless stated. Inputs are CP-1 and CP-1A figures; no source page was reopened.
| Item | Calculation | Result |
| Fixed-rate debt share | (500 + 760) / 1,966 | 1,260; 64.1 percent fixed; floating term loan 706 is 35.9 percent |
| Floating-rate sensitivity | 706 x 0.25 percent | 1.8, consistent with the filing's statement of about 2 per quarter-point |
| Maturity concentration | 500 / 1,966; 1,466 / 1,966 | 25.4 percent in 2029; 74.6 percent in 2031 |
| Offshore cash | 280 x 58 percent | About 162 outside the U.S. and about 118 in the U.S. (58 percent is itself approximate) |
| Tangible book equity | 1,017 - 858 | 159 |
| Claims outside debt, maximum of stated amounts | 60 + 78 + 66 + 17 + 27 | 248; gross debt plus 248 = 2,214 and over 372 = 5.95x (sensitivity, not a view) |
| Environmental liability net of escrow | 17 - 9 | 8 |
| Debt in years of free cash flow | 1,966 / 113 | 17.4 years at LTM free cash flow; indicative only because FY2025 includes the carve-out period |
| Net interest burden on sales | 151 / 3,284 | 4.6 percent |
| Fourth-quarter requirement | 90 - 32; 110 - 32 | 58 to 78 of free cash flow |
| Adjusted EBITDA add-backs | 372 - 250 | 122, or 32.8 percent of adjusted EBITDA |
## Gaps

Readiness status: READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS. Upstream status: CP-0 READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS, CP-1 accepted with limitations, CP-1A accepted and records READY_WITH_LIMITATIONS for this module, so confidence is below High. No Critical disclosure item was logged upstream.

### Evidence trace view

Magnera's analysis is traceable enough to support a view of its current debt, liquidity and earnings, and not yet a view of revolver access, covenant headroom or creditor legal capacity. Every citation quotation checked sits on the page it names, every derived figure recomputed from the filings equals the handoff, and unsupported claims are labelled as gaps rather than filled. The critical provenance gap is the executed debt documents and revolver terms: liquidity access, covenant headroom and legal capacity rest on no supplied source, and the credit view's Medium confidence depends on them. The affected decision is any view of usable liquidity or creditor control. The remediation owner is the sourcing step. Five minor defects need no change to any conclusion, and the review is a self-review by the host that wrote the handoffs.
